'''Margaret Buckingham''', {{post-nominals|country=UK|HonFRSE|post-noms=[[Foreign Member of the Royal Society|ForMemRS]]}} (born 2 March 1945) is a French-British [[developmental biologist]] working in the fields of [[myogenesis]] and [[cardiogenesis]]. She is an honorary professor at the Pasteur Institute in Paris and emeritus director in the [[Centre national de la recherche scientifique]] (CNRS).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.consulfrance-vancouver.org/Developmental-biologist-Margaret |title=Developmental biologist Margaret Buckingham is awarded the 2013 CNRS Gold Medal |publisher=Consulate General of France in Vancouver |access-date=4 November 2013 |archive-date=5 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161105220758/http://www.consulfrance-vancouver.org/Developmental-biologist-Margaret |url-status=dead }}</ref> She is a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]], the [[Academia Europaea]] and the [[French Academy of Sciences]].

== Biography ==
Margaret Buckingham was educated in [[Scotland]] and at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]] where she obtained B.A., M.A. and D.Phil. degrees in [[Biochemistry]]. As a postdoc, she then joined [[François Gros]] at the [[Pasteur Institute]] in [[Paris]] where she subsequently pursued her scientific career.  She is an honorary professor at the Pasteur Institute and emeritus director in the [[Centre national de la recherche scientifique]] (CNRS). She is a member of the scientific council of the [[European Research Council|ERC]]<ref>{{cite web|title=ERC|url=https://erc.europa.eu/erc_member/margaret-buckingham}}</ref> and chairs the prize committee of the Lefoulon-Delalande Foundation for cardiovascular research. In 2013, she was awarded the gold medal of the CNRS.<ref>[http://www2.cnrs.fr/presse/communique/3229.htm Communiqué de presse du CNRS] publié le 18 septembre 2013.</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Article La Croix, Médaille d'or du CNRS|newspaper=La Croix|date=18 September 2013|url=https://www.la-croix.com/Ethique/Sciences-Ethique/Sciences/La-medaille-d-or-du-CNRS-decernee-a-la-biologiste-Margaret-Buckingham-2013-09-18-1018816|archive-date=2019-08-20|access-date=2019-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820081811/https://www.la-croix.com/Ethique/Sciences-Ethique/Sciences/La-medaille-d-or-du-CNRS-decernee-a-la-biologiste-Margaret-Buckingham-2013-09-18-1018816|url-status=dead}}</ref> She is a member of the French Academy of sciences,<ref>{{cite web|title=Académie des sciences|url=https://www.academie-sciences.fr/fr/Liste-des-membres-de-l-Academie-des-sciences-/-B/margaret-buckingham.html}}</ref> a Fellow of the Royal Society of London/Edinburgh and an International member of the National Academy of Sciences USA. She is also a member of EMBO and of the [[Academia Europaea]]. She was a member of the scientific council of the [[European Research Council|ERC]] from 2016–2022. In addition to chairing the prize committee of the Lefoulon-Delalande Foundation, she also chairs the [[Pasteur Institute]] Ethics committee. She is currently a member of the scientific commission of the [[Curie Institute (Paris)|Institut Curie]] in Paris and of the scientific advisory board of the [https://hdbi.org/ Human Developmental Biology Initiative] in the UK.

She has French and British nationality, and is married to Richard Buckingham (Editor-in-Chief of ''Biochimie,'' until December 2020), with three children.

== Scientific research ==
Margaret Buckingham is a developmental biologist who is interested in how naïve multipotent cells acquire tissue specificity during [[Embryonic development|embryogenesis]]. She has studied both the formation of [[skeletal muscle]] and of the [[heart]], using the tools of mouse [[molecular genetics]] to characterise cell behaviour and to identify the [[gene]]s that govern cell fate choices.

Her main contribution to cardiogenesis is the identification of the second heart field (SHF) as a major source of cardiac progenitor cells that form specific regions of the heart.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kelly|first1=Robert G.|last2=Brown|first2=Nigel A.|last3=Buckingham|first3=Margaret E.|date=September 2001|title=The Arterial Pole of the Mouse Heart Forms from Fgf10-Expressing Cells in Pharyngeal Mesoderm|journal=Developmental Cell|volume=1|issue=3|pages=435–440|doi=10.1016/s1534-5807(01)00040-5|pmid=11702954|issn=1534-5807|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Buckingham|first1=Margaret|last2=Meilhac|first2=Sigolène|last3=Zaffran|first3=Stéphane|date=November 2005|title=Building the mammalian heart from two sources of myocardial cells|journal=Nature Reviews Genetics|volume=6|issue=11|pages=826–835|doi=10.1038/nrg1710|pmid=16304598|s2cid=28455128|issn=1471-0056}}</ref> The behaviour of these cells is controlled by gene regulatory networks and signalling pathways, exemplified by the ''[[FGF10]]'' gene.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Watanabe|first1=Y.|last2=Zaffran|first2=S.|last3=Kuroiwa|first3=A.|last4=Higuchi|first4=H.|last5=Ogura|first5=T.|last6=Harvey|first6=R. P.|last7=Kelly|first7=R. G.|last8=Buckingham|first8=M.|date=2012-10-23|title=Fibroblast growth factor 10 gene regulation in the second heart field by Tbx1, Nkx2-5, and Islet1 reveals a genetic switch for down-regulation in the myocardium|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=109|issue=45|pages=18273–18280|doi=10.1073/pnas.1215360109|pmid=23093675|pmc=3494960|issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref> Retrospective clonal analysis complemented their work on the SHF and established a lineage tree for the myocardium, where the second lineage defines the SHF contribution whereas the first lineage contributes all the [[Ventricle (heart)|left ventricular]] myocardium.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Meilhac|first1=Sigolène M|last2=Esner|first2=Milan|last3=Kelly|first3=Robert G|last4=Nicolas|first4=Jean-François|last5=Buckingham|first5=Margaret E|date=May 2004|title=The Clonal Origin of Myocardial Cells in Different Regions of the Embryonic Mouse Heart|journal=Developmental Cell|volume=6|issue=5|pages=685–698|doi=10.1016/s1534-5807(04)00133-9|pmid=15130493|s2cid=25041610 |issn=1534-5807|url=https://hal-pasteur.archives-ouvertes.fr/pasteur-02020731/file/DC%206%285%29685%E2%80%93698.pdf}}</ref> This analysis revealed the clonal relationships between different sublineages that contribute to both cardiac muscle at the poles of the heart and anterior skeletal muscles<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lescroart|first1=F.|last2=Kelly|first2=R. M.|last6=Buckingham|first6=M.|date=2010-09-07|title=Clonal analysis reveals common lineage relationships between head muscles and second heart field derivatives in the mouse embryo|journal=Development|volume=137|issue=19|pages=3269–3279|doi=10.1242/dev.050674|pmid=20823066|issn=0950-1991|doi-access=}}</ref> which are not under Pax3-control.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tajbakhsh|first1=Shahragim|last2=Rocancourt|first2=Didier|last3=Cossu|first3=Giulio|last4=Buckingham|first4=Margaret|date=April 1997|title=Redefining the Genetic Hierarchies Controlling Skeletal Myogenesis: Pax-3 and Myf-5 Act Upstream of MyoD|journal=Cell|volume=89|issue=1|pages=127–138|doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(00)80189-0|pmid=9094721|s2cid=18747744|issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free}}</ref> In addition to its conceptual importance for cardiogenesis, this work also has biomedical implications for congenital [[Congenital heart defect|heart malformations]].
